Higher demand for terraced homes as some buyers priced out of semi-detached segment: Huttons
article:
Semi-detached homes saw the biggest price jump among landed housing segments in the last quarter, despite lower volume.

Excluding Good Class Bungalows (GCBs) and strata landed homes, the prices of landed houses grew by 3.7% q-o-q in 3Q2026 to an average of $2,275 psf, URA data compiled by Huttons Data Analytics showed.

Overall volume and average price of landed homes

While all landed home segments saw price increases, the semi-detached segment recorded the biggest growth, rising 4.7% from an average of $1,989 psf in 2Q2026 to $2,082 psf in the last quarter.

Prices of terraced homes rose 2.7% q-o-q to $2,400 psf across the same period, while those for detached homes grew 1.4% to $2,046 psf.

This comes despite fewer semi-detached homes transacted. The segment saw 143 units sold in 3Q2026, falling 13.3% q-o-q. In contrast, terraced home sales remained steady in the last quarter — at 300 units, on a par with the 301 sold in 2Q2026.

Detached homes saw a slight decrease in sales volume, going from 50 units in 2Q2026 to 44 units in the last quarter.

“As some buyers were priced out of the semi-detached market, demand shifted towards terraced homes,” Huttons stated in its latest quarterly report on the landed market, published on Oct 26.

Transaction volume and average prices of landed homes by segment

In absolute terms, semi-detached homes were transacted at an average of $6.9 million in 3Q2026, rising 4.2% q-o-q. In comparison, prices of terraced and detached homes declined by 1.9% and 4.9% to $4.7 million and $13.0 million, respectively.

Overall, a total of 487 landed housing transactions were recorded in 3Q2023, excluding GCBs and strata landed homes. This is 5.6% less than the 516 deals logged in the previous quarter.

Huttons attributed the fall to seasonal factors that included the Lunar Seventh Month, along with slower activity in the HDB and private condo resale markets.

It added that rising land costs were prompting more buyers to opt for smaller landed properties. “The average land size of transacted landed homes shrank from 3,079 sq ft in 2Q2026 to 2,910 sq ft in 3Q2026,” the report stated.

In addition to smaller plots, landed homebuyers were also turning to shorter tenures, noted Lee Sze Teck, Huttons’ senior director of data analytics.

This comes amid a broadening price gap between freehold and 999-year leasehold homes compared to those with 99-year tenures.

“The price gap between 999-year leasehold/freehold and 99-year leasehold landed homes in 3Q2026 widened to 51.2%, the biggest since 2020,” he said.

As a result, there was a slightly higher proportion of 99-year leasehold landed transactions in the last quarter. These homes accounted for 15.6% of all landed housing deals in 3Q2026, up by 2.4 percentage points and the highest since 1Q2025.

Looking ahead, landed property volumes may “dip slightly” in 4Q2026 due to the year-end holidays, Lee noted. Nonetheless, backed by persistent demand, their prices should “stay firm”.

title: URA awards Marina Gardens Lane GLS site to EL Development at $1,243 psf ppr
article:
URA has awarded the tender for a Government Land Sale (GLS) site at Marina Gardens Lane to EL Development for $450.1 million, or $1,243 psf per plot ratio (psf ppr).

The tender for the residential site with ground-floor commercial space closed on Oct 15, with EL Development the sole bidder.

The developer’s offer fell below analysts' expectations of three to six bids and a top bid between $1,350 and $1,650 psf ppr.

The land rate is 11.3% lower than the $1,402 psf ppr Kingsford Group paid in 2023 for a neighbouring plot, which is now the 937-unit One Marina Gardens .

However, it is higher than the $984 psf ppr offer URA rejected in 2024 for a nearby GLS site at Marina Gardens Crescent. The sole bid by GuocoLand, Hong Leong Holdings and TID for the white site was deemed to be too low.

The Marina Gardens Lane plot awarded to EL Development measures 64,659 sq ft and has a maximum gross floor area of 362,119 sq ft. The 99-year leasehold site can yield about 390 homes and up to 1,615 sq ft of first-floor commercial space.

Based on the $1,243 psf ppr land rate, analysts predict future homes on the site could launch at average prices ranging from $2,500 to around $2,900 psf.

title: Shangri-La Singapore unveils refurbished Valley Wing with two Presidential Suites
article:
Shangri-La Singapore has unveiled its refurbished Valley Wing, with redesigned guest rooms and suites, including two Presidential Suites.

The luxury hotel’s refurbishment covered the Valley Wing's Executive Rooms, Executive Suites, Premier Suites and two Presidential Suites: the Shangri-La Suite and Singapore Suite.

Located within Shangri-La Singapore's 15-acre (6.07ha) grounds along Orange Grove Road, near Orchard Road, the Valley Wing has its own private driveway, lobby and check-in area, separate from the hotel's other accommodation wings.

Interiors inspired by Singapore's heritage

The redesigned interiors draw inspiration from Singapore's historic shophouses and tropical landscape, combining Asian decorative elements with European classical influences.

Geometric latticework, architectural mouldings and decorative panels reference traditional shophouse architecture.

Botanical wallpaper depicting tropical foliage, flowering branches and wildlife complements the soft greens, muted golds and warm neutrals used throughout the rooms and suites.

The Executive Rooms feature updated furnishings and seating areas, while the larger Executive and Premier Suites provide additional living space.

Two refurbished Presidential Suites

The largest accommodation in the hotel is the 348 sq m (3,746 sq ft) Shangri-La Suite, which has separate living and dining areas for private gatherings and entertaining.

The suite includes an upgraded 85-inch television, a private gym, its own lift and dedicated 24-hour butler service.

The second Presidential Suite, named the Singapore Suite, has two bedrooms, spacious living areas, panoramic views and a private whirlpool bath.

Both suites feature wall murals depicting tropical landscapes and floral designs, as well as upholstered furnishings and warm-toned interiors.

Exclusive facilities for Valley Wing guests

The Valley Wing retains its dedicated guest facilities, including the Summit Room, where breakfast is served, and the Valley Wing Lounge.

Guests can enjoy afternoon tea, champagne and refreshments at the lounge throughout the day, followed by evening cocktails and canapés.

“With this transformation, our vision was to honour the timeless elegance and sense of exclusivity that guests have come to cherish, while introducing a renewed expression of luxury that feels both contemporary and deeply connected to Singapore's heritage,” says Stephan Kapek, vice-president of operations and general manager of Shangri-La Singapore.

title: YZJ MARITIME: Why Chairman Ren Yuanlin Is Bullish About Next 8–10 Years
article:
Yangzijiang Maritime Development's 1H 2026 results presented a contrast: business is expanding rapidly, but profits are moving in the opposite direction.

Total income jumped
49% to US$81.6 million
, driven by a 70% surge in maritime income to US$51.7 million. Yet net profit attributable to shareholders fell 29% to US$44.9 million.

So when will this expansion pay off? Executive chairman
Ren Yuanlin
offered an answer at a 14 Oct Phillip Securities webinar: from 2027 through 2030.

A property developer — for ships

As background, Y

angzijiang Maritime Development traces its roots to
Yangzijiang Shipbuilding
, which listed on the SGX in 2007 and built up a substantial investment business.
In April 2022, Yangzijiang Shipbuilding spun off its investment arm as
Yangzijiang Financial Holding
.
Yangzijiang Financial subsequently expanded into maritime investments, including vessel financing, leasing and shipbuilding projects.
In November 2025, it spun off these maritime businesses into
Yangzijiang Maritime Development.
Listed on the SGX on 18 Nov 2025, Yangzijiang Maritime became the third listed company in the Yangzijiang family, led by veteran shipbuilder
Ren Yuanlin
.

An easy way to understand Yangzijiang Maritime is to think of a property developer, but for ships.
It arranges for vessels to be built at favourable prices, then sells them, sometimes before completion, or charters them out for recurring income.

The company works with second- and third-tier Chinese shipyards that have spare capacity but may struggle to attract international customers or secure refund guarantees.
Yangzijiang Maritime contributes technical expertise, vessel designs and procurement know-how.

Management says this combination can deliver building costs
up to 20% below prevailing first-tier shipyard prices
.

Ren said vessel sales typically earn profit margins of 15–20%, although construction takes two to three years. Importantly, that is not the same as a 15–20% annual return or group net profit margin.

A case study in the company's presentation illustrates the attraction: two vessels were sold before completion, generating more than US$20 million in combined profit.

Bullish assessment from industry veteran

Yangzijiang Maritime chairman Ren Yuanlin expressed confidence that the shipping and shipbuilding industry could enjoy another 8–10 years of strong business conditions, despite the weakness in China's economy and the broader global economy.

Drawing on his more than 50 years of industry experience, he gave three main reasons:

1.
Strong demand to replace ageing ships
. The need to replace ageing vessels will keep shipyards busy for years.
With many major shipyards already heavily booked, he sees limited capacity to accommodate additional demand, supporting a prolonged industry upcycle.

2.
Growing energy demand from AI.
Ren argued that AI's enormous electricity requirements would increase demand for energy, including oil and gas.
Transporting these commodities would support demand for tankers and other vessels.

3.
Geopolitical tensions are increasing shipping demand
. Conflicts and disruptions force vessels to take longer routes to avoid dangerous areas.
Consequently, ships take longer to complete voyages, reducing effective fleet capacity and supporting demand for additional vessels.

U

S$500 million of vessel sales

By August, Yangzijiang Maritime had signed 12 vessel sale contracts worth an aggregate
US$500 million
. Four involved newbuild bulk carriers. The US$500 million is gross contract value.

At the webinar, management outlined expected deliveries of nine vessels in 2026, 16–18 in 2027 and 24–26 in 2028, with the remaining pipeline extending into 2029–2030.

More deliveries should mean more opportunities for vessel sales and charter income. But they also create commitments to fund construction.

Why the profit squeeze?

Management acknowledged that the expanding business has pushed operating costs higher. It has also been moving vessels from time charters to spot charters to capture potentially higher freight rates.
Bringing charter vessels into operation can involve one-off startup costs of several hundred thousand US dollars per ship. Spot exposure may increase revenue in favourable markets, but also adds volatility.
And there was a major contributor: FX losses.
The swing in currency-related gains and losses was US$21.7 million, exceeding the US$18.6 million decline in reported net profit. DBS consequently estimated that profit excluding the FX effects actually rose about 7% year on year.

Bringing charter vessels into operation can involve one-off startup costs of several hundred thousand US dollars per ship. Spot exposure may increase revenue in favourable markets, but also adds volatility.

To share risks, Yangzijiang Maritime co-invests with established European ship operators, which commonly take equity stakes of 10–30%.
If resale prices are unattractive when vessels are completed, those partners can operate the ships to earn charter income instead.

A

Hong Kong possibility

Ren reiterated the company's guideline to distribute
40% of net profit as dividends
.

The company's balance sheet provides some reassurance.
At end-June, it had US$238 million in cash and net assets of approximately S$2.3 billion, equivalent to
60.87 Singapore cents per share
.

Ren also disclosed that management is exploring Hong Kong depositary receipts, which would allow investors in Hong Kong to trade an interest in Yangzijiang Maritime's shares without buying the shares directly on the SGX.  Nothing definite has been announced.

For shareholders, the central question is not how many ships Yangzijiang Maritime can order. It is how profitably — and how quickly — those ships can be monetised.

Ren expects a richer harvest from 2027. The challenge now is to turn the expanding vessel portfolio into higher profits and cash flow — and demonstrate that shareholders' patience is justified.

title: Top 3 Temasek-Linked Blue-Chip Stocks to Watch This Week
article:
This week, three prominent
Singapore blue-chip companies
with Temasek Holdings as a substantial shareholder will update investors across three consecutive days.
Mapletree Industrial Trust
(SGX: ME8U), or MIT, goes first on 27 October 2026.
Mapletree Logistics Trust
(SGX: M44U), or MLT, follows right after on Wednesday, 28 October 2026.
Keppel Ltd
(SGX: BN4) wraps up the trio on 29 October 2026.

Temasek, a global investment company headquartered in Singapore, held a deemed interest of 34.3% in MLT and 27.4% in MIT as at 29 May 2026, and 21% in Keppel as at 31 March 2026.
These three names share far more than just a major shareholder.
Each has spent the past year selling assets.
This week, we find out whether those sales are showing up in the numbers income investors care about.
Can MIT stop the slide in North America?
For the first quarter of the financial year ending 31 March 2027 (1QFY2027), MIT’s distribution per unit (DPU) fell 4.9% year on year (YoY) to S$0.0311.
Gross revenue slipped 7.7% to S$162.3 million, while net property income (NPI) dropped 8.5% to S$122.3 million.
Some of that was expected, since MIT sold three Singapore properties in August 2025.
However, lease non-renewals in North America and a weaker US dollar added to the drag.
North America remains the sore spot.
Occupancy there fell to 82.5% from 86.1% three months earlier.
On a brighter note, Singapore occupancy picked up to 94.3% from 93.4%, and Japan stayed fully occupied.
Overall occupancy slipped to 90.7%.
On the flip side, DPU rose 0.6% from the preceding quarter.
MIT signed around 364,500 square feet of leases in North America, including a 10-year lease with an aerospace technology company at Hawthorne Data Centre.
The
real estate investment trust
(REIT) also sold its Philadelphia Data Centre for US$14.5 million, securing a price about 4% above its US$13.9 million valuation.
So, what should you watch on 27 October?
Check whether the quarter-on-quarter DPU gain holds and whether North American occupancy stops falling.
Look, too, for progress on its target of S$500 million to S$600 million in divestments in that market, and for any move in aggregate leverage from 37.5%.

Will MLT’s asset sales lift its DPU?
MLT, which holds 175 logistics properties across nine Asia-Pacific markets, had a steadier quarter.
In 1QFY2027, its DPU rose 0.2% YoY to S$0.01816.
Gross revenue expanded 0.8% to S$178.9 million, while NPI rose 2.0% to S$156.4 million.
MLT picked up income from a Grade A warehouse in Mumbai and a full quarter’s contribution from Mapletree Joo Koon Logistics Hub.
Softness in China and broader Asian
currency headwinds
ate into some of those gains.
Excluding currency effects, and gross revenue would have grown 2.0% and NPI 3.1%.
China shows up in the rental numbers too.
Rental reversion across the portfolio was a positive 0.9%.
Take China out, and it rises to 2.3%.
Occupancy dipped to 96.4% from 96.9% three months earlier.
After the quarter, MLT announced three divestments worth around S$155 million.
Two China properties will go to a Mapletree-led RMB fund, while 39 Changi South Avenue 2 in Singapore will be sold at 20.3% above its valuation.
On 28 October, follow those proceeds.
Aggregate leverage held at 40.5%, higher than MIT’s, and any debt repayment would show up there first.
Meanwhile, the average cost of debt stayed at 2.6%.
Related articles:

STI Downturn: 3 Temasek-Linked S-REITs to Watch
Can Keppel’s asset-light engine outrun its legacy losses?
For the first half of 2026 (1H2026), Keppel grew revenue 24.6% YoY to S$3.8 billion.
However, net profit attributable to shareholders went in the opposite direction, dropping 59.0% to S$154.7 million.
The main culprit behind that drop was a heavy S$375 million loss registered in its non-core portfolio, driven by legacy rig impairments and the terminated sale of telco M1.
Excluding that legacy portfolio, core net profit expanded 25% YoY to S$530 million.
The core business kept growing.
Recurring income rose 13% YoY to S$467 million.
Funds under management (FUM) reached S$106 billion as at 30 July 2026.
Keppel had originally targeted S$100 billion by the end of 2026, meaning it crossed that finish line early.
Next up: S$200 billion by 2030.
Here’s the thing: profit is not cash.
Keppel’s operating cash flow fell to S$96.8 million from S$219.4 million a year ago as working capital requirements expanded.
As at 30 June 2026, the group held S$2.2 billion in cash against S$11.3 billion in borrowings, excluding lease liabilities.
Keppel paid an interim dividend of S$0.150 per share on 21 August 2026, unchanged from a year ago.
When Keppel updates the market on 29 October, start by reviewing its progress on asset monetisation.
At its half-year results, Keppel had announced around S$1.7 billion in asset sales against its S$2 billion to S$3 billion full-year target.
Then check whether the non-core portfolio throws up more losses and whether operating cash flow picks up.

title: Want S$3,000 a Month in Retirement? Here’s How CPF LIFE and Dividend Stocks Can Work Together
article:
You want S$3,000 a month in retirement.
You start doing the maths.
At a 4% dividend yield, you’ll need S$900,000 invested to generate that income.
That’s when retirement starts to feel rather expensive.
But what if you don’t actually need S$900,000?
What if part of your retirement income is already taken care of?
That’s where CPF LIFE comes in.
By combining CPF LIFE payouts with dividends from Singapore stocks and real estate investment trusts (REITs), you could reduce the amount your investment portfolio needs to generate.
And as we’ll see, the difference could be worth hundreds of thousands of dollars.
How Much Can CPF LIFE Pay You Every Month?
CPF LIFE provides monthly payouts for as long as you live, helping Singaporeans manage the risk of outliving their retirement savings.
How much CPF LIFE pays you depends on your Retirement Account savings, the plan you choose and when you start receiving payouts.
CPF has three retirement sum reference levels: Basic Retirement Sum (BRS), Full Retirement Sum (FRS) and Enhanced Retirement Sum (ERS).

CPF LIFE provides lifelong monthly payouts, while dividend stocks offer the potential for additional income and capital appreciation.
There are important differences in how much flexibility and certainty each provides.

For instance, CPF LIFE could help cover essential household expenses, while dividend income provides additional flexibility for discretionary spending.
The aim isn’t necessarily to choose one over the other, but to understand what each can contribute to your retirement income plan.
Should You Put More Money Into CPF or Dividend Stocks?
This is where
retirement income planning
becomes more personal.
Additional CPF retirement savings can increase your eventual lifelong payouts. CPF LIFE also offers an Escalating Plan, which starts with lower payouts that increase over time.
However, CPF savings are subject to withdrawal restrictions.
Dividend investments offer greater flexibility because you can generally sell your shares when you need access to capital, although doing so during a downturn could mean accepting losses.
Consider two investors targeting S$3,000 monthly.
One might prefer to build up CPF savings for higher lifelong payouts. Another might prioritise an accessible investment portfolio, accepting the possibility of fluctuating dividends and share prices.
The appropriate balance depends on your existing CPF savings, retirement timeline, liquidity needs and willingness to take investment risks.
Don’t Let a High Dividend Yield Fool You
Remember our earlier calculation?
To generate S$14,640 annually, you would need S$366,000 invested at a 4% dividend yield.
At 6%, you would need just S$244,000.
That’s S$122,000 less investment capital.
Tempting, isn’t it?
But there’s a reason investors shouldn’t chase the
highest dividend yield
.
A yield can rise simply because a company’s share price has fallen. If earnings weaken or debt becomes harder to manage, that attractive yield may not last.
For investors building retirement income from Singapore dividend stocks and REITs, three questions matter:
Can the business sustain its dividends?
Examine earnings, cash flow, debt and payout commitments.
Is your income diversified?
Relying heavily on a few banks or REITs could expose your portfolio to sector-specific problems.
Can you manage uneven payouts?
Dividends may arrive quarterly or half-yearly, so cash reserves can help cover monthly spending.
A sustainable 4% yield may ultimately serve your retirement needs better than a 6% yield that gets cut, although neither outcome is guaranteed.
How to Build Your S$3,000 Monthly Retirement Income Plan
Start by estimating your monthly retirement expenses, then check how much CPF LIFE could provide using CPF Board’s
Retirement Payout Planner
.
Next, calculate your remaining income gap and assess whether your investment portfolio can realistically generate the difference.
Finally, consider whether your investments are sufficiently diversified and whether their income can remain sustainable through different market conditions.
Reaching S$3,000 a month in retirement isn’t necessarily about accumulating a S$900,000 dividend portfolio.
Depending on your CPF LIFE payouts, the amount your investments need to generate could be considerably smaller.
The challenge is building that additional income without taking unnecessary risks simply to chase higher yields.
A good retirement plan isn’t about making every dollar work harder. It’s about making sure each source of income has a job to do.

title: European gas hits €97 for first time since 2022 on winter risks
article:
(Oct 26): European natural gas topped €97 a megawatt-hour for the first time since 2022 as concerns mount about the region’s fragile supply balance this winter and the outlook for the Middle East conflict.

Benchmark futures extended last week’s advance by as much as 3.5% early Monday. Traders expect an uptick in heating demand in the coming days, with temperatures set to drop across the continent. That would coincide with tight global gas supplies and set the stage for bidding wars with other buyers, such as Asia.

Expectations are fading that the market could ease any time soon amid continued hostilities and supply disruptions in the Persian Gulf. Iran is bracing for a fresh US bombing campaign around America’s November midterms and is preparing to retaliate across the Middle East, Bloomberg News reported.

Volatile liquefied natural gas flows have played a crucial role in supplying Europe’s energy since the 2022 crisis, leaving it vulnerable to potential disruptions as the continent enters its peak-demand season with abnormally low fuel inventories. EU gas-storage sites are about 75% full, the lowest for the season in records going back to 2009, while those in Germany are at just over 61%.

European gas prices are still well below the peaks of the last energy crisis but the latest advance risks fanning inflation and weighing on economic activity. So far in October, Europe’s LNG imports have lagged last year’s levels despite typically jumping this time of year.

See also: Oil declines from six-month high as traders assess Mideast risks

Dutch front-month futures, Europe’s gas benchmark, traded 3.2% higher at €96.88 a megawatt-hour by 8.50am in Amsterdam. As a result of the rising gas prices, French month-ahead power futures exceeded €200 a megawatt-hour for the first time since January 2023.

title: Palantir’s fast-selling US$170 windbreaker shows its Korea appeal
article:
(Oct 26): Palantir Technologies Inc has spent years selling governments and companies its data analytics. In South Korea, it’s also selling US$170 ($217) windbreakers — and they are flying off the shelves.

Thousands of fans descended on a two-storey pop-up store in Seoul last week to snap up hoodies, T-shirts and hats bearing Palantir’s logo, with a Korea-exclusive windbreaker selling out within hours.

The frenzy underscores an unusual level of enthusiasm for a company better known elsewhere as a secretive military and surveillance contractor that has faced protests over its work with the US military and immigration authorities.

Palantir has increasingly sought to cultivate that fandom. It has released everything from tennis whites to a US$239 French chore coat, using merchandise to build a more approachable public identity around a company whose core products most consumers will never encounter.

“We take the merchandise very seriously,” said Eliano Younes, Palantir’s head of engagement. “For a lot of these folks, the only time they’ll ever really get to touch Palantir is through the merchandise.”

That strategy has found greater success in South Korea where the government and some of its biggest industrial companies are pouring money into artificial intelligence. Sales from last week’s event jumped 30% from 2025, while the country has at times ranked as Palantir’s second-largest market after the US for online merchandise, according to Younes.

See also: Musk claims US$40 bil chips debt closed, yet talks ongoing

That enthusiasm matters because Korea is emerging as one of Palantir’s promising avenues for overseas growth. chief executive officer Alex Karp last year called the country the “second most interesting market” after the US.

The fandom also offers Palantir a way to cultivate a broader and more approachable public identity as it expands globally. The company has faced criticism over its handling of data and its ties to the Donald Trump administration.

But in Seoul, the company is making gradual inroads.

See also: OpenAI resumes training AI — without internet access

Since opening its South Korean office in 2022, Palantir has been expanding its presence. Last week, it signed a deal with Posco Future M to accelerate its AI-driven transformation. It also struck partnerships with Korean telecommunications giant KT in March 2025 and defence firm LIG Nex1 in March.

Dan Do, who works in the dental industry, has been a Palantir investor since it went public in 2020. Drawn initially to the company’s “defend the West” narrative and government business, he later saw potential in its Foundry commercial software. His frequent posts about Palantir on X earned him early access to the Seoul event, which he flew from Sydney to attend.

“The company puts a lot of effort into building community,” said Do, clutching an armload of streetwear to buy.

In Korea, public and corporate enthusiasm for AI is high. Seoul’s trend-driven consumer culture also gives Palantir an opportunity to present itself not simply as a defence contractor but as a technology brand with a devoted following, said Yoon Young-bin of OAAH Agency, an experience-curation service.

The country is home to globally important semiconductor, shipbuilding, automotive and manufacturing companies — all potential partners for Palantir, which is seeking to embed its AI and data software. The government is also accelerating spending on artificial intelligence, tripling its AI budget this year to 10.1 trillion won (US$7.6 billion or $9.8 billion) as it embraces the concept of sovereign AI.

The latest merchandise to drop was a Korea-exclusive white nylon windbreaker that would “look really nice on the golf course”, said Younes, adding that the sport’s popularity in Korea factored into its development.

The inaugural Seoul pop-up last year attracted more than 5,000 fans over two days. The response prompted Palantir to increase inventory this time, impose limits on how many items each visitor can buy and introduce pre-registration. Even so, some products quickly sold out.
