Flashing an emblem can also foster a shared identity, helping brands form and expand fandoms, said Kim Yong-seok, the CEO of Talksulting, a brand-strategy firm.

In Palantir’s case, “the main consumers are likely to be individuals who find the potential of Palantir’s technology to resonate, investors who have high hopes for the company’s future and fans who have developed an affinity for the brand itself”, Kim added.

title: Chinese carmakers overtake Japan in Europe for first time
article:
(Oct 26): Chinese automakers outsold Japanese rivals in Europe for the first time over a full quarter, underscoring how quickly brands like BYD Co and Chery Automobile Co are gaining ground in the region.

Registrations of Chinese-branded cars roughly doubled from a year earlier in September to make up 12.7% of total sales across the region, led by hybrids, according to market researcher Dataforce. That’s put them ahead of Japanese manufacturers including Toyota Motor Corp at 11.9%.

While European manufacturers like Volkswagen AG or Renault SA still dominate the region, the speed of China’s surge has been a surprise. Five years ago, Chinese brands accounted for barely 1% of European sales. Japan’s automakers, by contrast, have spent decades building their position in Europe.

Toyota has sold cars in the region since 1963 and now operates factories across the continent, while Nissan Motor Co has produced vehicles at its Sunderland plant in the UK since 1986. China’s offering is especially successful in the UK, where Chery’s Jaecoo 7 SUV was the country’s best-selling model in March and September.

The shift is a double whammy for Europe’s struggling manufacturers. China’s drivers are deserting VW and BMW AG in their biggest market in favour of domestic rivals, who are churning out new models faster and at lower cost. And shrinking demand in China is forcing BYD and others to look for new markets.

Earlier this month, Chery, BYD and Geely’s Zeekr showed off a range of new models at the Paris car show, offering well-priced cars like the BYD Dolphin G DM-i, a compact plug-in hybrid specifically developed for Europe. Bringing their EV lineups to Europe also positions them to benefit from a jump in demand as fuel prices hit record highs.

The European Union is trying to temper an expansion that is partly fuelled by state-backed subsidies. After adding extra tariffs on China-made battery-electric vehicles, the bloc this month agreed in principle to curb fast-growing imports of hybrid cars from China.

See also: Nextdc CEO to forgo bonus after Australia data centre delay

Amid speculation of future measures, shipments of hybrids have accelerated.

Separately, the EU is considering new rules that would favor locally made cars when granting subsidies and other incentives. The proposals include linking some company-car tax benefits to European production, a powerful tool in many countries like Germany where corporate and fleet buyers dominate.

Carmakers like Mercedes-Benz Group AG have welcomed the political backing, but warned of distortions to global supply chains, driving costs up. Countries including the UK, Türkiye and Morocco ship vehicles and parts to the EU that could struggle because of Made in Europe rules.

Chinese manufacturers have been preparing to produce locally already. Chery is preparing production in Barcelona and BYD is nearing the completion of a manufacturing site in Hungary. Zhejiang Leapmotor Technology Co has started making its B10 SUV at Stellantis NV’s plant in Zaragoza, Spain, as part of the companies’ joint venture.

title: Food-delivery firm Meituan aims to raise US$1 bil in bond sale
article:
(Oct 26): Chinese food-delivery giant Meituan is seeking to raise the equivalent of about US$1 billion through its offshore yuan bond offering, according to people familiar with the matter, as it joins a growing wave of issuers tapping the dim sum debt market.

The company has obtained approval from Chinese regulators to raise a larger amount offshore but decided to preserve part of the quota for dollar bond refinancing when market conditions are favourable. Meituan representatives told investors during a call on Monday, the people said, asking not to be identified discussing private matters. The quota is set to expire next September, they added.

The dim sum bond offering is expected to be priced on Tuesday, the people said.

Meituan is raising the debt as competition has eased in China’s food delivery and retail business following a crackdown by authorities, taking some pressure off the sector’s big players. The firm reported a surprise quarterly profit in August and has also slowed its overseas expansion.

Proceeds from the sale, which is the company’s second-ever dim sum bond offering, will be used mainly to refinance offshore yuan-denominated loans, the people said.

Meituan raised about US$3 billion from a sale of dollar securities and offshore yuan notes last year in its largest regular bond issuance ever. It expects capital expenditure to reach around RMB20 billion in 2026 and increase modestly in 2027, according to the people.

See also: Chinese copper titan He Jinbi jailed for life over Maike fraud

Yuan financing has become increasingly appealing to both Chinese and foreign firms for its lower costs. Government and corporate issuers have sold over RMB1 trillion of dim sum notes outside mainland China this year, an all-time high, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. Earlier this month, Tencent Holdings Ltd raised RMB26 billion of such notes, surpassing its dollar tranche in a single offering for the first time.

Like its Chinese tech peers, Meituan has developed its own large language models for artificial intelligence, called the LongCat series. But the company isn’t updating its AI offerings as fast as rivals such as Alibaba Group Holding Ltd or ByteDance Ltd.

title: Bitcoin dips below US$80,000 as AI-related market selloff deepens
article:
(Oct 26): Bitcoin retreated below US$80,000 on Monday as broader risk-off sentiment ahead of a Federal Reserve meeting and concerns over the artificial intelligence trade weighed on cryptocurrencies.

The largest digital asset fell as much as 1.4% to under US$79,300 before paring some losses to trade around US$80,000 in afternoon trading in Asia. Smaller tokens including Ether, XRP and Solana also declined. The moves came after investors pulled US$772.4 million from US-listed spot bitcoin exchange-traded funds on Thursday and Friday, a sharp reversal from more than US$1 billion of net inflows earlier in the week.

The declines accompanied a broader market slump that extended from last week as investors questioned massive spending on AI and looked toward this week’s earnings reports from tech giants for clues about the outlook. The Kospi Index in South Korea — a bellwether for the AI trade — fell 0.2% and chip-related stocks were among the biggest decliners in Japan’s Nikkei.

“Bitcoin has so far been relatively resilient to the AI debt concerns that are weighing on all risk assets,” said Caroline Mauron, co-founder of Orbit Markets. “The market focus is now on the Fed meeting, followed by the US midterm elections.”

Bitcoin remains in the risk-off basket for many systematic funds and algorithmic traders, leaving it vulnerable to deteriorating sentiment, said Pratik Kala, portfolio manager at Apollo Crypto.

See also: Bitcoin falls below US$83,000 as AI jitters weigh on sentiment

Kala pointed to online discussions about AI, including comments from SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk about potential consolidation next year, as contributing to market strain. Advances in AI have also exacerbated potential security risks for crypto, making some investors skittish, he added.

title: Chinese PCB maker Dongshan raises US$1.3 bil in HK listing
article:
(Oct 26): Suzhou Dongshan Precision Manufacturing Co, a printed circuit board maker, raised about HK$9.9 billion in Hong Kong’s biggest listing in nearly two months, which hit a volatile market for companies related to the artificial intelligence build out.

The company priced about 113.8 million shares at HK$86.80 apiece, compared to a maximum of HK$93.80, according to a filing to the city’s stock exchange on Sunday, which confirmed an earlier Bloomberg News report. Dongshan said it had not exercised an upsize option. Trading is expected to begin on Oct 28. The price represents a discount of about 35% to the Friday close of its Shenzhen-listed stock, which is up 35% this year even after a nearly 60% slide from a June peak.

Dongshan, which makes the components that are the intricate electronic backbone of AI servers, is braving the market at a tricky time across Asia, especially for companies in its business.

First-time listings have raised more than US$50 billion in Hong Kong this year, edging closer to the US$57.8 billion record set in 2010 but rising bond yields and poor deal performance are making investors and issuers more cautious. A string of withdrawals and delays, including by major data centre operators in the region, has prompted some companies to put near-term listing plans on hold.

“With Dongshan’s Shenzhen share price declining substantially, the reference valuation for its Hong Kong offering has also fallen,” said Francis Tan, Asia chief strategist at Indosuez Wealth Management in Singapore. “Investors still want exposure to the AI revolution but they are increasingly demanding earnings visibility rather than simply buying the narrative.”

See also: Hong Kong IPO red flags include sudden loans and secret handshakes

The company’s Shenzhen-listed shares dropped as much as 5.6% in early Monday trading.

Chinese technology stocks have been particularly hit hard, with no end in sight for a deepening selloff as investors confront the realities of an economy that’s weak enough to erode corporate profits but not to trigger forceful new stimulus.

The world’s second-largest equities market has lost US$3.5 trillion in value from a peak in May, data compiled by Bloomberg show. The rout intensified last week, pushing the onshore benchmark CSI 300 Index into a bear market and a technology sector gauge in Hong Kong toward erasing all its gains since Beijing’s sweeping growth support package two years ago.

Dongshan Precision’s listing leaned heavily on cornerstone investors, which get guaranteed allocation in the deal in exchange for holding the stock for at least six months. They include JPMorgan Asset Management, Alibaba Group Holding Ltd, CPE and Montage Technology Co, who agreed to buy a combined 50% of the offering. Jane Street Group and Jump Trading LLC are also among them.

The Suzhou-based company makes PCBs and optical transceivers, key components for AI. It’s the third-largest PCB supplier in an US$85.2 billion global market, according to its prospectus.

UBS Group AG, Guotai Haitong Securities Co, GF Securities Co and Citic Securities Co are joint sponsors for the Hong Kong listing.

title: Jio’s record India IPO falls short of record payday for bankers
article:
(Oct 26): Jio Platforms Ltd raised a record amount of funds for billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s digital and telecommunications giant but it proved to be far less lucrative for the bankers handling the deal.

The company is paying about 1.96 billion rupees in fees to the 19 banks on the roughly US$3.1 billion IPO, according to filings. That amounts to about 0.65% of the issue size, trailing the fee pools of several previous offerings in India.

Fierce competition among investment bankers in India has compressed fees, particularly for marquee deals. Firms are often willing to accept thinner economics for a coveted role in high-profile transactions. The payoff can instead come through league-table rankings, bragging rights and credentials that help win the next big pitch.

That is a far cry from the days when Hyundai Motor India Ltd paid about 4.9 billion rupees to bankers for its then-record 278 billion-rupee IPO in 2024. Paytm parent One 97 Communications Ltd paid about 3.2 billion rupees for its 183 billion-rupee offering in 2021 while Swiggy Ltd handed out about 2.8 billion rupees for its 113 billion-rupee share sale.

Those types of windfalls have been elusive of late. National Stock Exchange of India Ltd, another blockbuster IPO this year, paid about 1.9 billion rupees to a syndicate of 20 banks that worked on its roughly US$2.4 billion offering, equivalent to about 0.8% of the issue size. Bankers split fees of just 46.3 million rupees for SBI Funds Management of India Ltd’s billion-dollar offering in July.

See also: JSW Steel’s 2Q profit more than triples on higher prices

Investor enthusiasm, meanwhile, has been anything but restrained. Jio’s IPO was fully subscribed within the first 100 minutes of bidding and had attracted bids for nearly 22 times the shares on offer by Friday, according to BSE Ltd data.

title: Musk claims US$40 bil chips debt closed, yet talks ongoing
article:
(Oct 26): Elon Musk said SpaceX has closed a US$40 billion ($51 billion) debt deal to pay for the chips it needs to fuel its artificial intelligence (AI) ambitions. People familiar with the discussions, though, told Bloomberg News that talks over pricing were still ongoing.

“SpaceX closed $40B of debt for GPUs,” Musk wrote in a post on X, referring to Nvidia Corp’s graphics processing units. He went on to suggest that debt markets had all but shut for neoclouds depending solely on revenue streams from AI data centres. “That means the 200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation,” Musk wrote. “Some will make it through, but not many.”

Musk’s comments came on the heels of a tumultuous week for the AI industry in debt markets as concern mounted over the rapid spending, and limited profits so far to show for it. With investors demanding increasingly large premiums to finance the AI buildout, the volatility roiled pricing discussions over the SpaceX debt, which is being structured as private bonds to be issued by an off-balance sheet entity.

As of late Sunday in New York, those conversations remained ongoing and the deal hadn’t priced, people with knowledge of the discussions said. The parties are still working on finalising the debt package in the coming days, they said.

More broadly in markets recently, much of the investor angst has been focused on the so-called neoclouds, which sell high-end computing power to technology companies. Noting SpaceX’s revenue from its Starlink business and rocket launches, Musk sought to differentiate his company from those businesses.

“As of the past few weeks, debt markets have almost entirely shut off access to money for any company that doesn’t have substantial revenue independent of AI data centres,” Musk said in his post. He later said that SpaceX won’t buy any neoclouds, calling it “pointless”.

See also: OpenAI resumes training AI — without internet access

SpaceX, which is rated investment-grade by the three largest credit graders, has seen the price of its own debt tumble in recent weeks. Credit-default swaps tied to SpaceX, which are used to insure against losses on the company’s debt, surged last week to a record 266 basis points at the close of trading Friday, a level more typical of a junk-rated borrower.

Bankers led by Goldman Sachs Group Inc have been discussing the chips debt structure with investors led by Apollo Global Management Inc, with Apollo-backed Atlas SP slated to manage the entity, people familiar with the matter said last week, asking not to be identified discussing private information. Pacific Investment Management Co has also considered investing, according to the people. The debt was expected to be issued in the form of private placements called 144a, the people said.

With the latest structure, SpaceX would avoid a repeat of a financing attempt last year by Musk’s AI startup, xAI. In that deal, an entity sought as much as US$20 billion of off-balance sheet debt through a sale-leaseback agreement with Valor Equity Partners. But SpaceX ultimately had to record about US$13 billion of that debt after it was declared a “failed sale-leaseback arrangement”, according to SpaceX’s latest earnings report.

The debt raise comes after strong third quarter earnings, with SpaceX’s AI unit turning a profit for the first time. The enterprise is increasingly driving revenue by selling computing power from its Memphis data centres to external AI labs and hyperscalers.

During SpaceX’s earnings call, chief financial officer Bret Johnsen indicated that the company was in discussions with lenders over further borrowing.

“We have a lot of conviction that we are going to be able to do this in a very measured fashion and continue to keep ourselves in that IG status along the way,” he said, pointing at the firm’s investment-grade rating.

title: Chinese copper titan He Jinbi jailed for life over Maike fraud
article:
(Oct 26): He Jinbi, one of the biggest names in Chinese copper trading, has been sentenced to life in prison over fraud and other offences committed by the company he founded, Maike Metals International Co.

A court in the western Chinese city of Xi’an found Maike guilty of contract fraud, bribery and other offences last month, and handed its 61-year-old boss, He, a life sentence, according to people familiar with the verdict. The ruling found Maike’s conduct had exposed several Chinese banks to more than US$1 billion of potential losses, the people added, asking not to be named due to the sensitivity of the issue.

He — whose company was forced into restructuring in 2023 after a liquidity crisis stemming from Covid-19-era disruptions — has appealed the verdict. Members of the family, the defence team and He himself did not respond to Bloomberg telephone calls and voice messages.

The judgment has not been made public. While China does have online databases for most legal proceedings, political and other exceptions for sensitive cases can allow courts to hold back publication.

He Jinbi’s defence, argued during proceedings that neither the company nor its founder intended to commit fraud. Maike worked with banks for more than a decade and regularly repaid its loans, striving to do so even when upheaval due to pandemic restrictions reduced cash flows. At least some losses at the lenders stemmed instead from inadequate internal risk controls and procedures, they said.

A personable, charismatic figure, He was part of a group of enterprising traders who made fortunes during the rush for commodities in the early 2000s, as China began to urbanise and develop at a breakneck pace. Maike, which he had founded with friends in Xi’an in 1993 with a RMB50,000 loan (close to US$8,700 at the time), shifted from mechanical and electrical products to focus on scrap metal, copper wire and refined copper.

See also: Food-delivery firm Meituan aims to raise US$1 bil in bond sale

Maike built a position as a key link between international miners, traders and buyers. At its peak, the group handled one in every four tonnes of copper imported into the world’s top consumer of the metal.

The company placed bold bets, becoming a pioneer in the practice of borrowing against the massive volumes of metal He was shipping and storing in warehouses. Maike was also at the forefront of a trend that saw many Chinese conglomerates expand into the booming real estate sector, investing in the hotels and business centres.

In 2022 the company’s finances came under pressure as Covid-19 restrictions upended business and a downturn in China’s property market hurt its investments. A sharp fall in copper prices added to the strain. He acknowledged that year that Maike had sought help to address a liquidity crisis.

See also: Sinking profits turn China’s US$3.5 tril stock rout into trap

As Maike struggled to meet its obligations, creditors began taking action. In October 2023, Maike executives reported losing touch with He, and believed he had been detained by police. Maike filed for bankruptcy the following month.

Xiamen Xindeco Ltd, a state-owned company and one of Maike’s major creditors, won a bid to lead the restructuring of Maike and 25 affiliated companies, according to an exchange filing last December.

Xindeco said it would invest RMB285 million in cash. Under the plan, one of its units would take a 75% stake in a newly formed company consolidating Maike’s remaining trading and logistics assets, including facilities in Shanghai’s free-trade zone and offices in Shanghai, Xi’an and Shenzhen. A bankruptcy service trust in Shaanxi province will hold the remaining 25%, the company said in December.

title: BYD’s Korea expansion challenges Hyundai dominance on home turf
article:
(Oct 26): When Lee Seongdong decided to replace his 2016 Chevrolet Spark in April, a two-year wait for Hyundai Motor Co’s Casper Electric was already pushing him toward BYD Co’s Dolphin. He was so impressed by the feature-rich ride that he signed a contract on the spot.

The price was attractive too: the Dolphin hatchback starts at 24.5 million won (US$18,500 or $24,000), though discounts meant Lee paid less than 23 million won — similar to a subsidised Casper Electric, which can be bought at about 22 million won in Seoul, but only in its bare-bones trim. Combined with not having to wait for longer than South Korea’s mandatory military service to take delivery, the 47-year-old YouTuber said the BYD was “way too good to pass up”.

Lee’s purchase is part of a burgeoning shift underway as BYD brings its low-cost strategy, which is already winning it market share in Europe, to increasingly price-sensitive buyers in South Korea. Bloomberg Intelligence’s data shows a ninefold jump in BYD’s EV and hybrid sales from January to August to almost 18,000 units, as Hyundai’s comparable sales fell 6% to about 139,000.

The momentum extended into September, when BYD’s registrations hit 20,000 — double its initial goal for the year, according to Korea Automobile & Mobility Association data.

BYD’s rapid ascent means it’s overtaken Volvo and Toyota Motor Corp in the ranks of foreign carmakers in Korea — a significant milestone given it only entered the passenger car market in early 2025 and, in July, lost access to government subsidies after not meeting some requirements. That’s a growing risk to local heavyweights Hyundai Motor Co and Kia Corp, which despite still holding a combined 72% share of the domestic market, are struggling to compete with the lower-priced, technology-focused models on offer by BYD.

See also: Chinese market is gone for Western automakers, says Volvo CEO

For the first time since 2010 — excluding the 2020 pandemic slump — Hyundai’s annual global sales will likely fall below four million units, missing its 4.16 million target, according to Samsung Securities Co analyst Esther Yim.

“The biggest driver of their slowdown is Chinese competition,” Yim wrote in a recent note. “Chinese EV makers’ aggressive export push has ignited intense price wars everywhere except the US and India, and Hyundai and Kia are underperforming in all those markets.”

Chinese automakers are accelerating their push into Korea. BYD is broadening its lineup with the Sealion 6 DM-i plug-in hybrid at 37.5 million won, the cheapest in its segment. Geely Automobile Holdings Ltd’s premium brand Zeekr began deliveries of its 7X electric SUV last week after surpassing 1,500 preorders, while XPeng Inc and Chery Automobile Co have set up local entities ahead of their market debuts.

See also: Porsche locks-in on the super-sportscar segment with the Mission S

Speaking at an event this month, Lee Jae-kyu, a senior vice-president overseeing vehicle development at Hyundai Motor Group, said he felt “despair” at the design and pricing edge Chinese automakers displayed at the recent Paris Motor Show.

“While European carmakers presented uninspiring designs and technology, Chinese vehicles offered superior design at prices roughly US$10,000 cheaper,” Lee said. “I couldn’t shake the thought that European companies will go under soon, and even our group is structured in a way that it could eventually be swallowed by China.”

Despite BYD’s rapid gains, analysts say Chinese brands face long-term hurdles due to sparse service infrastructure, high repair costs, steep insurance premiums and swift depreciation. In online driver communities, BYD owners regularly complain about spare parts delays and high repair bills, with minor bumper and fender benders exceeding 11 million won in some cases.

BYD plans to expand its South Korea service locations to 26 from 20 by the end of this year. The Shenzhen-based company’s low-price strategy will ultimately be tested against Hyundai and Kia’s network of more than 1,200 domestic service centres, according to Brian Lee at CLSA Securities Korea Ltd.

“Right now, everyone is focused purely on the sticker price,” he said. “But as the market matures and resale value, service access and maintenance costs become clear, their overall appeal could fade.”

Still, expansion in new foreign markets is critical for Chinese automakers as they face slowing demand at home, growing barriers in Europe, and are effectively shut out of the US. In contrast, Korea imposes an import tariff of just 8% on Chinese passenger cars and in August excluded EVs from a bill granting tax credits to domestic manufacturers, leaving Hyundai and Kia with few policy shields against cheap Chinese imports.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

Last month, KAMA — representing South Korea’s five automakers also including GM Korea, Renault Korea and KG Mobility — urged parliament to pass tax incentives and policy support.

“The penetration of Chinese EVs could trigger the collapse of not just domestic EV makers, but the entire auto industry,” the group warned in a statement.

Growing concerns over China’s rapid push have prompted South Korean lawmakers to introduce a bipartisan bill this month proposing tax credits covering up to 50% of annual domestic production costs for strategic industries, including EVs.

For buyers like Lee, the Dolphin owner, the broader policy worries mirror what he sees in the market: Chinese brands are raising the competitive bar.

“I hope our domestic auto industry succeeds, but in the end, you have to win through open market competition,” Lee said. “Everyone needs to stay alert and compete.”

title: Sembcorp explores supplying low-carbon power to Singtel’s Nxera
article:
Sembcorp Industries’ utilities unit has signed a memorandum of understanding to explore supplying renewable and low-carbon energy to Singtel’s Nxera data centres in Singapore.

They will assess power generation using low-carbon hydrogen or biomethane, solar panels fitted vertically to buildings, and electricity imported from a floating solar development at Linggiu Reservoir in Johor, Malaysia.

“AI is driving a step-change in the power needs of data centres, and in a land- and resource-constrained market like Singapore, how we source that power matters. Working with Sembcorp gives us more options to power our growth sustainably and responsibly,” says Bill Chang, CEO of Nxera and Singtel’s Digital InfraCo unit.

The Johor development is planned to have about 2.2 gigawatts of peak solar capacity. In August, Sembcorp received conditional approval for a 300-megawatt import project supported by the development, which it expects to begin operating in 2029.

“With a proven track record of powering the data centre sector, Sembcorp is well-positioned to support this growth through our diversified energy portfolio. Our partnership with Nxera further affirms our shared ambition to enable the next generation of digital infrastructure while advancing the global energy transition,” says Koh Chiap Khiong, president & CEO, Gas and Related Services and CEO of Singapore of Sembcorp.

The companies exchanged the MoU at Singapore International Energy Week on Oct 26 in the presence of Dr Tan See Leng, Minister for Energy, Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry), Singapore and Datuk Amar Haji Fadillah bin Haji Yusof, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Energy Transition and Water Transformation, Malaysia.

title: RBA warns retirement wave will test Australian pension funds
article:
(Oct 26): Australia’s central bank has warned the nation’s A$4.8 trillion (US$3.4 trillion or $4.3 trillion) pension industry is facing a fresh set of challenges as millions of people enter retirement over the next decade and funds face cash outflows as people draw down their savings.

The so-called superannuation sector has become a large owner of domestic assets and has historically been a “countercyclical stabilising force”, in times of market stress such as the Covid-19 pandemic, Reserve Bank of Australia Assistant Governor Brad Jones told the AFR Super and Wealth Summit in Melbourne on Monday.

Jones said weekly net inflows of A$1 billion-A$2 billion have historically helped the sector absorb stress. He warned that cushion may become less dependable over time as more funds move into net cash-outflow positions as more people retire and draw on their savings. About 2.5 million people are expected to retire over the next decade.

“When we look at all of that, what have been some very powerful tailwinds are going to start to become headwinds and just require more astute management,” Jones said, adding he was also concerned about concentration among some of the service providers in the industry, including funds’ administration.

Jones declined to answer a question on whether the RBA is set to hike interest rates again at its meeting next week.

Executives from two of the nation’s largest super funds, Aware Super and Australian Retirement Trust, said they had prioritised their liquidity management in anticipation of more members entering retirement and potential market shocks.

See also: 42% of Singapore respondents will only start planning for retirement within five years of their planned retirement date

“Even in the way that we’re structuring our investment team, we have deliberately put in a head of liquidity looking and focusing in on a lot of these issues” that are related to both retirement savings but also market stresses, Aware Super CEO Deanne Stewart told the same panel.

title: Challenger rejects Daiichi Life’s US$4.4 bil takeover offer
article:
(Oct 26): Challenger Ltd’s board rejected a US$4.4 billion offer from Daiichi Life Group Inc, saying it intends to engage with the Japanese insurer’s Australian unit to see whether a proposal can be reached that the board can recommend.

Challenger said there’s no certainty that a binding offer or transaction will materialise, after an indicative bid from TAL Daiichi Life Australia wasn’t at a level it could recommend to shareholders, according to a statement Monday.

Daiichi Life’s Australian unit last week offered to buy the remaining 79.5% of Challenger at A$11.80 per share, valuing the financial firm at about A$7.9 billion (US$5.5 billion).

Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Matt Ingram said Challenger’s sum-of-the-parts is above the bid. “A revised offer of A$12.50-A$13 per share might be more agreeable” to the board, he wrote Monday.

Shares of Challenger and Daiichi Life were little changed on Monday.

Japanese insurers have been making acquisitions overseas as a shrinking population constrains growth at home. Daiichi Life and Sumitomo Life Insurance Co were among bidders for the Singaporean insurance unit of HSBC Holdings Plc, though Allianz SE eventually emerged as the buyer. Sompo Holdings Inc bought Aspen Insurance Holdings Ltd for about US$3.5 billion earlier this year.

See also: Nextdc CEO to forgo bonus after Australia data centre delay

Established in 1985, Challenger managed about A$128 billion in assets as of the end of March, according to its website. The company is Australia’s largest provider of annuities in the nation’s retirement market.

title: Oil declines from six-month high as traders assess Mideast risks
article:
(Oct 26): Oil retreated as the US and Iran stuck to familiar rhetoric in their conflict, and a technical gauge pointed to overbought conditions.

Brent fell below US$115 a barrel after surging to a six-month high last week, while West Texas Intermediate was near US$101. US President Donald Trump told Fox News it’s “getting to be decision time” on whether he will make a deal with Tehran or “finish it off”. Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said “they will not attempt” an attack if rationality existed, referring to the US.

On the technical front, Brent’s 14-day relative-strength index — a measure of the pace and magnitude of price movements — topped 74 on Friday. That’s above the level of 70 that some traders see as signalling a pullback.

Brent has still surged almost 90% this year as the war in the Middle East disrupted flows and drew in Yemen’s Houthi rebels, who have been targeting Saudi Arabia. Investors are braced for several major events that could move markets, with Israeli elections due Tuesday, followed by the US midterms in early November. Between the two, the Federal Reserve sets monetary policy.

In recent days, Washington ordered a wider evacuation of diplomatic personnel from across the Middle East, while President Trump has hinted his forces could resume strikes after the US midterms on Nov 3. For its part, Iran is preparing to retaliate, including against Israel and the United Arab Emirates, according to a person familiar with the Islamic Republic’s thinking.

At the weekend, there was further fighting between Iranian-backed Houthis in Yemen and Saudi Arabia, ratcheting up risks to energy flows. The rebel group claimed that they targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh in response to Saturday’s Saudi attacks in Sanaa and other areas in Yemen.

See also: Singapore to store Saudi crude: Tan See Leng

“The rise in fighting in the region, combined with the worries that escalation is around the corner, mean that oil markets need to price in the risk of oil and refined-product inventory depletion,” Commonwealth Bank of Australia analyst Vivek Dhar said in a note. “We see Brent oil futures needing to rise as high as US$150 a barrel to compel uncontrolled demand destruction, where high prices force lower demand, in emerging Asian economies.”

At present, crude shipments from the Middle East have recovered to near prewar levels, including through the Strait of Hormuz, despite Iranian attacks on vessels. The narrow waterway links the Persian Gulf to global markets, and has been at the centre of the conflict.

More than 1.5 billion barrels of crude have passed through Hormuz with American assistance “since summer”, according to US Central Command, which oversees Washington’s military operations in the region. Its forces have both imposed a full blockade of Iranian ports to choke its shipments, while assisting passages for other Persian Gulf producers’ vessels.

See also: Eni raises investor payouts as high fuel prices boost cash flow

“The market is pricing in some risk of escalation after the US midterm elections, when Washington may feel less constrained by the immediate political cost of higher oil prices,” said Jorge Leon, head of geopolitical analysis at Rystad Energy AS. “That risk could keep prices elevated even if flows improve.”

The US and Israel began the war with an attack in late February, with the stated aim of ending Iran’s nuclear ambitions. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu — who has been endorsed in the election by Trump — said in a campaign video released on Saturday Tehran was renewing the programme.
• Brent for December settlement shed 1.8% to US$114.58 a barrel at 10.30am in Singapore.

title: Nextdc CEO to forgo bonus after Australia data centre delay
article:
(Oct 26): Nextdc Ltd’s chief executive officer will give up his short-term and long-term bonuses for the 2027 financial year after the Australia data centre developer warned delayed power supply at one of its major projects in Melbourne would hit profits.

“The board and management are focused on two priorities: working with our customer and the electricity distributor to minimise the impact of the M3 power delay, as well as earning back the confidence of our investors and other stakeholders,” chairman Douglas Flynn said in a statement ahead of the company’s annual general meeting next month.

Flynn and the company’s non-executive directors agreed to a 10% reduction in their fees, the statement said, adding that the board had also withdrawn a resolution to seek shareholder approval to increase the maximum annual remuneration of non-executive directors to A$2.5 million, from A$2.2 million

CEO Craig Scroggie will not receive any cash or other award in place of his relinquished incentives.

Last week’s news of the delay at the company’s M3 data centre in the Western suburbs of Melbourne prompted the biggest drop in its share price since the company listed in 2010.

Flynn reaffirmed his intention to retire from the board once a new chairman is in place, after a short handover period.

See also: Chinese manufacturer Dongshan raises US$1.3 bil in HK listing

Global search and board advisory firm Spencer Stuart has been hired to find an independent non-executive director and a new chair, according to the statement. The new board members will ideally have data centre, energy or infrastructure development and capital management experience, Nextdc said.

title: Singapore shields itself from energy risks as Indonesia cuts gas
article:
(Oct 26): Singapore is diversifying suppliers, adding storage and building new infrastructure to try to protect itself from growing risks of resource nationalism, Singapore’s Minister for Energy, Trade and Industry Tan See Leng said in a speech on Monday.

The remarks came as Indonesia began reducing natural gas exports to the city-state from Saturday, as Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto seeks to bolster domestic supply. Singapore’s Energy Market Authority has said the country has sufficient supplies and that the cuts represent less than 2% of its total daily gas demand, and Tan said there is no concern of shortages.

“We can keep calm and carry on,” he said at the Singapore International Energy Week conference. “Our households and our businesses can be assured that our energy security is always at the top of our minds.”

Singapore plans to add more liquefied natural gas capacity to import from a wider array of suppliers, build new power plants and increase fuel stockpiles to guard against potential disruptions, Tan said.

“Singapore will not be able to insulate ourselves from global or regional shocks,” he said. “When there is a supply crunch, countries may also prioritise their own domestic needs, and this trend of resource nationalism is particularly concerning.”

While Indonesia is a major gas exporter, overseas shipments have declined in recent years as a growing share of output is directed to domestic use. Major liquefied natural gas markets include China, Japan and South Korea, while pipeline natural gas is sent to Singapore and Malaysia.

See also: Sembcorp Industries has ‘potential direct exposure’ to Indonesia’s natural gas supply cuts: JPM, DBS

Indonesia is a top supplier of gas to Singapore — which depends on the imported fuel for nearly all of its power generation — but the island has significantly reduced its dependence on pipeline supplies in recent years as LNG shipments have grown.

“About half of our gas is imported as LNG from a global diversified portfolio of sources, such as the US, Africa, the Middle East, and Australia,” Tan said.

The country expects to increase its LNG throughput capacity by another 50% once its second import terminal comes online ahead of 2030, he said.

See also: Indonesia begins trimming pipeline gas exports to Singapore

The country announced plans to build five new power plants coming online between 2026 and 2031 that will increase generation capacity by more than a quarter.

Tan separately announced a non-binding agreement between Saudi Arabia and the city-state to store Saudi crude oil in caverns beneath Jurong Island from the second half of 2027.

title: Mapletree Investments completes transition to self-management of UK student housing assets
article:
Mapletree Investments has completed integrating its externally managed UK student housing asseets under its in-house operator, Student Castle, which manages close to 17,000 beds in the country.

“Self-management forms a core component of our long-term strategy for markets where we have sufficient scale. The successful transition to self-management for our UK portfolio underscores our disciplined execution and sets the groundwork for a similar move for our US student housing portfolio,” says Matt Walker, CEO of Mapletree’s student housing arm.

“Self-management gives us full control over the resident experience and asset performance – two critical drivers of success in this highly specialised and operational sector,” adds Tom Rix, chief operating officer of Student Castle.

Student Castle was acquired by Mapletree in April 2024 for GBP1 billion. The portfolio includes 31 student housing assets across the UK and Germany.

As at March 31, Mapletree’s global student housing portfolio comprises 76 assets with over 25,000 beds across 40 cities in the US, UK, Canada, Germany and Australia.

title: Sembcorp Industries has ‘potential direct exposure’ to Indonesia’s natural gas supply cuts: JPM, DBS
article:
Sembcorp Industries (SCI) (SGX:U96 ) is likely to be affected by Indonesia’s move to restrict natural gas exports to Singapore, say analysts from JP Morgan and DBS. Shares of SCI are down by 4.66% since the market opened on Oct 26 and the company is currently trading at $5.73 as of 10:03 am.

Since Oct 24, Indonesia has cut pipeline gas exports to Singapore by 31 billion British thermal units per day (BBTUD). The reduced amount comprises 15 BBTUD from West Natuna and 16 BBTUD from Jambi Merang, South Sumatra. Indonesia’s oil and gas regulator SKK Migas said the cuts were made to shore up its domestic energy supplies.

The move came just days after Indonesia’s Coordinating Minister for Downstreaming and Energy Transition Bahlil Lahadalia said he would not hesitate to halt energy exports to countries that do not respect Indonesia. Bahlil did not name any country.

Singapore’s Coordinating Minister for National Security and Minister for Home Affairs K Shanmugam told reporters on Oct 19 that the city-state will “use every legal and regulatory lever at our disposal” to hold companies responsible for the transboundary haze coming from Indonesia.

According to Tan See Leng, Singapore’s Minister for Energy, Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry), the cuts are unlikely to affect Singapore’s electricity prices in the short term. This is because the reduction makes up less than 2% of Singapore’s energy needs.

This was the same assessment made by JP Morgan and DBS analysts who note that while Singapore will be able to manage the near-term disruption and shortfall, the city-state may still have to grapple with higher replacements costs and further supply cuts down the line.

See also: Singapore shields itself from energy risks as Indonesia cuts gas

“SCI is likely to be more affected, as its pipeline gas is sourced largely from West Natuna, while its 50%-owned Senoko and Keppel source piped gas from Malaysia,” DBS says in its Oct 26 note. “Both SCI and Keppel have secured significant long-term contracts with gas-cost pass-through mechanisms, supported by hedges, to mitigate gas-price fluctuations.”

That said, the companies still have some exposure to shorter-term contracts ranging from one to two years, DBS says. For instance, most of Senoko’s contracts are shorter than five years. This makes their plants more exposed to power-spread volatility. “The optimism on power companies following rising power spreads in recent months, could be dampened by this latest development,” DBS adds.

JP Morgan, on the other hand, says that the disruption in Indonesian natural gas supply could be supportive for recontracting as legacy customer contracts roll off for both SCI and Keppel. That said, both companies were not able to qualify the earnings impact during JP Morgan’s initial discussions with them. “This remains an evolving situation,” JP Morgan says.

See also: Indonesia begins trimming pipeline gas exports to Singapore

Although SCI has “potential direct exposure” to the cuts through Sembcorp Gas’s West Natuna supply arrangements, JP Morgan says the company has a diversified gas portfolio that spans piped natural gas (PNG) and liquefied natural gas (LNG). Notably, SCI’s long-term LNG supply is contracted through 2042 and 80% of its ex-Senoko-gas-fired capacity is contracted for at least five years.

This will reduce SCI’s direct exposure to movements in the short-term Uniform Singapore Energy Price (USEP), Singapore’s wholesale price for electricity, and fuel prices, JP Morgan adds.

On Oct 26, the Energy Market Authority, which regulates Singapore’s electricity and gas sectors, gave Sembcorp Utilities conditional approval to import a total of 1.3 gigawatts of electricity to Singapore. The SCI subsidiary is working with its consortium partners in MY Energy Consortium (MYEC) to source and integrate low-carbon electricity from regional sources such as offshore wind from Vietnam and solar power from Malaysia.

Aside from Sembcorp Utilities, the MYEC’s members include Petronas, Tenaga Nasional Berhad and Petrovietnam Technical Services Corporation.

As for Keppel (SGX:BN4 ) , JP Morgan expects its exposure to be mitigated because its gas is predominantly sourced from Malaysia. The bank expects Keppel’s earnings for 2HFY2026 to be supported by its newly commissioned Sakra plant and the progressive deployment of $13.5 billion in new private fund mandates.

“Any near-term knee-jerk share price reaction should be cushioned by a mid-4% yield and faster-than-expected non-core monetisation, including legacy rigs and Keppel South Central, with Keppel on track to deliver its FY26 disposal target of $2 to $3 billion.”

Keppel shares are trading 0.6% higher at $10.06 as of 10.03 am.

title: Lim Han Kwang to succeed John Ng as YTL PowerSeraya CEO
article:
YTL PowerSeraya has announced that deputy CEO Lim Han Kwang will succeed incumbent CEO John Ng with effect from Jan 1, 2027, marking the culmination of a planned leadership transition that began more than two years ago.

The integrated energy company says that the planned succession ensures continuity of strategy, stewardship and operational excellence as YTL PowerSeraya enters its next phase of growth and supports Singapore’s energy transition.

Ng will remain as a director of the company’s board, providing professional experience, industry knowledge and strategic counsel that contribute to YTL PowerSeraya’s business.

With more than four decades of commercial and operational experience across Singapore’s energy sector, Ng was appointed CEO of the YTL PowerSeraya for the second time in January 2019, returning to an organisation he had helmed from 2009-2013. Prior to his second stint, he served as CEO of Singapore LNG Corporation.

During his latter CEO stint, Ng led the company to record profits, including the firm’s top three most profitable financial years ever. He also oversaw the acquisition of the 396 MW Tuaspring Power Station in June 2022 and the award to YTL PowerSeraya of the first request for proposal under the Energy Market Authority’s centralised process to develop a 600 MW hydrogen-ready combined cycle gas turbine.

Francis Yeoh, chairman of YTL PowerSeraya and executive chairman of YTL Power International describes Ng’s achievements to go beyond financial performance. He says: “He [Ng] has brought judgement, conviction and an unwavering sense of duty to every chapter of the company’s growth, from strengthening our generation portfolio to advancing future-ready investments that support Singapore’s energy transition. His career stands as an example of leadership grounded in experience, service and purpose.”

See also: SGX should begin planning ahead for ‘eventual transition’ in CEO role: SGX’s Loh Boon Chye

“My journey with the organisation has spanned many important moments, from its earlier PUB days to the YTL PowerSeraya of today,” says Ng. “I am proud of what we have achieved together, particularly in strengthening the group’s performance, expanding our generation capabilities and investing in infrastructure that will support a more secure and sustainable energy future.”

Yeoh also welcomed Lim as CEO-designate, saying: “His [Lim’s] deep understanding of Singapore’s energy landscape, strong regulatory and commercial experience, and proven leadership at Geneco position him well to lead YTL PowerSeraya into its next phase. This succession reflects our commitment to continuity, disciplined execution and long-term value creation for our stakeholders.”

Working in Singapore’s electricity and gas markets for more than 23 years across various roles, Lim brings with him a wealth of experience. “I am honoured to be entrusted with the responsibility of leading YTL PowerSeraya into its next chapter,” he says. “John has built a remarkable legacy defined by resilience, strategic clarity and service to the industry, and I am grateful for his mentorship and continued guidance on the board.”

See also: XMH Holdings to appeal $10.2 mil tax bill for FY2024; slapped with $12.5 mil tax for FY2025

The succession of Lim to the role of CEO follows a deliberate transition process that began in 2024, when he was promoted to deputy CEO of YTL PowerSeraya while continuing in his role as CEO of Geneco.

Lim adds that he will focus on building the “strong” foundation established by Ng and the team, while advancing YTL PowerSeraya’s role as a trusted integrated energy company that supports Singapore’s evolving energy needs, while contributing “meaningfully” to the nation’s net zero ambition.

title: Singapore to store Saudi crude: Tan See Leng
article:
Saudi Arabia and Singapore are working to establish an arrangement for Saudi crude oil to be stored at the Jurong Rock Caverns from 2H2027 onwards, announces Tan See Leng, Minister for Energy, Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) on Oct 26.

Speaking at the Singapore International Energy Week (SIEW), Tan says that the arrangement enhances the resilience of the Saudi crude oil supply chain in Southeast Asia as well as contributing to the city-state’s energy security and resilience in the event of supply disruptions.

Jurong Rock Caverns is the first commercial underground rock caverns facility for the storage of liquid hydrocarbons in South-east Asia. Located at a depth of 150m below the ground, and 130m beneath the Banyan Basin on Jurong Island, JRC can store up to 1.47 million m3 of liquid hydrocarbons such as crude oil and condensate.

Saudi Aramco will sign a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with the Energy Market Authority and JTC Corporation, with negotiations scheduled to conclude in a “few” months time, adds Tan.

title: Stocks under pressure before earnings, oil dips
article:
(Oct 26): Stocks struggled to recover from a volatile week as investors awaited megacap earnings for clues on whether the recent pressure on the artificial intelligence (AI) trade will persist. Crude oil fell.

MSCI Inc’s Asia Pacific equities gauge swung between small gains and losses in early Monday trading after posting its fourth consecutive decline last week, the longest losing streak since April.

Futures contracts for the S&P 500 Index and the Nasdaq 100 Index pared early gains and were little changed after the AI trade came under intense pressure last week and a key US chip gauge posted its longest weekly losing streak since November.

Meanwhile, a Tokyo-based exchange-traded fund tracking Brazilian stocks slumped 12% after Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva pulled off a surprising win in Sunday’s runoff.

Providing some support, global crude oil benchmark Brent dropped 1.1% from a six-month high to about US$115.40 a barrel. US President Donald Trump said it’s “getting to be decision time” on whether to reach a deal with Tehran or resume attacks as threats from Iran and the Houthis against Americans in the Middle East mount.

Investors face another pivotal week after a volatile stretch for the AI trade, with earnings from Microsoft Corp, Alphabet Inc and Amazon.com Inc set to test confidence in the sector. Federal Reserve and Bank of Japan policy decisions will add to the week’s major catalysts as officials contend with stubborn inflation, higher energy costs and elevated bond yields globally.

See also: Swiss stocks becoming a haven from AI fears roiling markets

“Global markets are preparing for another big week,” Nick Twidale, chief market analyst at AT Global Markets in Sydney, wrote in a note. The focus is “set to shift back towards central banks and interest rates after several weeks of geopolitical headlines dominating market moves”.

The Fed and its peers in the eurozone and Japan will probably keep rates steady in the coming week, opting to bide their time before potential further hikes. Three days of decisions starting on Wednesday in Washington are likely to affirm a hawkish stance balanced by a measured pace as policymakers confront inflation risks ranging from surging energy prices to the AI boom.

The US central bank raised rates in September for the first time since 2023 and signalled another increase was likely this year. While US inflation has remained elevated, officials have indicated little urgency to move again this week, with economists and investors expecting the next increase in December.

See also: Stocks fall as oil rally keeps a lid on Treasuries

Elsewhere, French bond futures climbed after the country dodged a downgrade at Moody’s Ratings, providing respite for a country beset by surging bond yields, political gridlock and street protests.

The euro was also quoted a touch higher. Gold slipped 0.2% to about US$3,990 an ounce.

It’s also Asia’s busiest earnings week. About 550 of the roughly 1,200 companies in the MSCI Asia Pacific Index are due to report this week, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. That includes some of the biggest names in the AI boom, such as Korean memory giants SK Hynix Inc and Samsung Electronics Co.

Geopolitical risks are also likely to remain elevated heading into next month. Trump has suggested US strikes on Iran could resume after the Nov 3 midterm elections, while officials have warned the period between the vote and the new Congress taking office could be particularly dangerous.

The US is reducing diplomatic and military staffing in parts of the Middle East as threats from Iran and the Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen increase. The Houthis have repeatedly targeted Riyadh airport, which reopened Sunday for commercial flights.

“Several factors collide in the week ahead that could determine how the markets fare for the rest of 2026,” wrote Kyle Rodda, a senior analyst at Capital.com in Melbourne.

title: Keppel gives Seatrium contract worth 'over' $500 mil to complete four legacy rigs
article:
Keppel has given Seatrium a contract worth "over" $500 million to complete the construction of four offshore rigs.

These four rigs are now part of the portfolio of ten so-called "legacy" rigs that Keppel is holding under an entity called RigCo, following the merger of Keppel's offshore and marine unit into then Sembcorp Marine, now renamed Seatrium.

Via RigCo, Keppel maintains the flexibility to complete, sell, or lease these legacy rigs.

The construction cost of these four rigs will be funded using cash now held under RigCo, reads a joint announcement by the two companies.

These rigs comprise a premium seventh-generation drillship, a harsh environment jackup, and two mid-water semisubmersibles suited to work in the harshest environments of Northwest Europe.

The drillship and the harsh environment jackup are expected to be delivered to RigCo in 2027 and 2028 respectively, while the construction plans for the remaining two rigs are being assessed.

See also: Seatrium to undertake ninth FSRU conversion project for Karpowership

The two companies note in their joint statement that following more than a decade of limited newbuild activity and the progressive retirement of older rigs, offshore rig market fundamentals are improving.

Cindy Lim, CEO, Infrastructure, of Keppel, and non-executive director of RigCo says that demand for deepwater and harsh environment rigs is expected to increase over the next several years, providing conducive conditions for new, long-term charters of premium rigs.

"RigCo has been working closely with customers on their requirements amid the tightening market for advanced offshore rigs," she adds.

"The resumption of construction work marks an important milestone in Keppel's strategy to transform RigCo’s work-in-progress offshore rigs into high-quality, income-generating assets," says Lim.

"We are pleased to work with Seatrium, leveraging their world-class engineering and construction capabilities, to complete and deliver these rigs with high specification, on time, within budget, and safely," says Lim.

William Gu, executive vice president of Seatrium Energy (Marketing), notes that more than two-thirds of the world's operational jackup rigs are based on Seatrium's designs, including one of the units for RigCo.

"This award reflects our undisputed capabilities to deliver complex projects safely, efficiently and to the highest quality standards.

"We look forward to leveraging our integrated capabilities and execution excellence to support RigCo in realising the full potential of these premium assets," he adds.

title: The Assembly Place to invest up to $2.5 mil in living sector fund managed by ICHAM
article:
A subsidiary of Catalist-listed co-living operator The Assembly Place (TAP) will invest up to $2.5 million in a living sector fund managed by Singapore-based multi-family office and alternative asset fund manager ICHAM, according to an Oct 26 bourse filing.

ICHAM will serve as the investment manager of the fund and will be responsible for managing and operating the fund, while TAP is both an investor as well as the proposed property manager and operator of the fund’s property assets.

The fund has a target size of $300 million. TAP did not detail the portfolio of the living sector fund, instead stating that the fund “will benefit from TAP’s operating expertise and track record across Singapore’s community living sector”.

ICHAM is an affiliate of the ICH Group, co-founded by former Yangzijiang Financial CEO Vincent Toe. The fund manager holds a capital markets services licence for fund management issued by the Monetary Authority of Singapore.

As at June 30, ICHAM managed approximately US$686 million ($876.91 million) in assets across private equity, fixed income and hybrid strategies with a network spanning Singapore, Thailand, China, Hong Kong and Japan.

TAP CEO and executive director Eugene Lim say the move represents “another extension of our asset-light strategy”. “We are pleased to participate in the fund as both an investor and the proposed property manager and operator of its property assets. Our investment demonstrates our alignment with the fund and its investors, while our strategic involvement allows ICHAM and the fund to draw from TAP’s track record and expertise in enhancement and management of living sector assets.”

See also: US mortgage bond funds suffer one of worst outflows since 2021

Toe, investment manager of ICHAM, says Singapore’s living sector is “underpinned by resilient demand fundamentals, evolving lifestyle preferences and growing demand for flexible, professionally managed accommodation”.

He adds: “ICHAM aims to leverage on TAP’s expertise and track record in the community living sector in Singapore to unlock differentiated value propositions of the fund’s real estate assets and maximise asset value. With TAP’s sectoral expertise and operational support, we aim to establish a strong foundation for the fund’s expansion in the living sector, creating enduring value through operational excellence, disciplined growth and new investment opportunities.”

Founded in 2019 and listed on the Singapore Exchange in 2026, TAP manages over 3,520 keys across 103 property assets in Singapore, with more than 2,100 additional keys in its development pipeline.

Its portfolio spans six living sectors: residential co-living, hotels and serviced apartments, student accommodation, foreign healthcare professionals' accommodation, inter-generational living and migrant workers’ accommodation.
